Issued at 1120 AM CDT Mon Sep 14 2026

This Afternoon - Tuesday Morning: Periods of Heavy Rain

Multiple waves of moderate to heavy rainfall affect the local 
area over the next 24 hours. This first broad but not 
necessarily intense wave of rain currently upstream over 
southwestern MN and western Iowa lifts into the region through 
the day as the associated zone of theta-e advection likewise 
lifts northeast. While the mid-level tropical Pacific moisture 
river will be in place by midday, the lower tropospheric Gulf 
airmass lags behind by 4-6 hours, resulting in deep tropical 
rainfall processes not being fully realized until late this 
afternoon and tonight. 

This late afternoon to overnight timeframe--with PWATs near 2" 
and deep warm cloud depths of 10-12 kft (climatological highs 
for this time of year)--is the period worth watching for higher
rainfall rates and potential flooding impacts. The good news is
that soils are dry heading into this event and the rainfall 
looks to be on the progressive side with enough breaks between 
each round to reduce the overall risk of any flooding. By 
Tuesday morning, there is a solid signal in the CAMs that most 
areas should see total rainfall amounts around 1" with localized
pockets of 2-3", with these corridors driven by the tracks of 
the individual small convective cells containing the higher 
rain rates (a 20-30% shot that a given location will fall under
one of these higher rainfall swaths). A cold front pushing 
southeastward overnight will also aid in keeping the heavy rain 
corridors fluid in space and gradually shifting off to the 
southeast of the area by mid- morning Tuesday.


Later in the Week: The Rain Returns, Could be Heavy

Broad subtropical upper tropospheric ridging builds across the 
southern and southeastern U.S. in the wake of our passing shortwave 
tonight into Tuesday, lingering well into the weekend. This feature 
and the attendant surface ridge act to keep the lower 
tropospheric baroclinic zone from sliding too far south of the 
forecast area for Tuesday into Wednesday, with the surface to 
700-mb front likely pivoting over northern Missouri and southern
Iowa Tuesday night as a northern stream wave approaches along 
the U.S./Canadian border and lee cyclogenesis takes place along 
the Front Range. The mid-tropospheric front returns to the 
region by Wednesday afternoon, which could serve to generate 
elevated showers. Similar to this afternoon, the deeper moisture
lags to the south and doesn't arrive until Wednesday night into
early Thursday. Therefore, any rain on Wednesday does not look 
to be of much impact. 

The zonal flow and subtleties of any upper level forcing make 
the timing and amounts of any rainfall for Thursday difficult to
nail down. Nevertheless, the thermodynamic environment will be 
primed and ready to produce efficient rainfall rates should the 
forcing come to fruition. At this point, the threat for heavier 
rainfall is progged to be south of I-90.

There is an increasing signal for Friday and the weekend that the 
upstream pattern amplifies as a cutoff low begins to advance 
eastward out of California. This facilitates a greater risk for 
heavy rainfall, which will be dictated by the placement of near 
surface baroclinic zone--lifting northward during this time 
towards central Minnesota/Wisconsin. The recent EPS/GEFS runs 
are honing in on this Friday into Saturday period for the next 
widespread heavy rain potential with 40-50 percent of the EPS 
members exceeding 2 inches for total rainfall amounts and upper 
end ensemble members exceeding 3-4 inches. Given the strength of
this signal and the stronger synoptic forcing at play, it is 
more of a question of where, rather than if, this heavy rain 
occurs. Such details will be refined over the next few days 
given that this event is still 5-6 days out. One cannot also 
fully rule out the risk for stronger storms on Friday afternoon
and evening depending, again, on how far north the surface 
front tracks.

What we can say with higher certainty is that temperatures should 
remain solidly in the 60s and 70s for highs through the week, a 
solid taste of late summer/early fall weather.
